screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts: Sending Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll move beyond reading contract data and learn how your DApp sends transactions that actually change state. Sending a transaction means creating a signed Ethereum transaction, paying gas, and waiting for the network to mine it. You'll learn what parameters are required — such as the sender address, value for payable functions, and gas limits — and how wallets like MetaMask participate by asking the user to sign. We'll walk through a practical example using a SimpleStorage contract's setNumber function, show how to estimate gas and add a safety buffer, and how to read the transaction receipt to confirm success. Along the way you'll learn common failure modes: user rejection, insufficient funds, out of gas, and reverted transactions, and how to present clear feedback to users. By the end you'll be able to implement a setStoredNumber workflow in your DApp that validates input, estimates gas, triggers MetaMask, monitors confirmation, and recovers gracefully from errors. Think about transactions as the paid, deliberate actions your users take on-chain — designing clear, safe flows reduces confusion and costly mistakes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Sending Transactions
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Send transactions that change state

We demonstrate building a DApp flow that requests a signed transaction, estimates gas, and reads the transaction receipt to confirm success.

Estimated time: 10–15 minutes
Why it matters

Transactions are how users change state: mint tokens, transfer value, or update contract storage. Proper handling protects user funds and UX.

Common outcomes

Pending → mined (confirmed) or failed (revert/out of gas). User rejection stops signing and throws a code 4001 error.

Explore Key Topics
Transaction Parameters
from, value, gas, gasPrice or EIP-1559 fields.
Gas Estimation
Estimate and add a buffer to avoid out-of-gas fails.
Receipt & Confirmation
Read receipt.transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and event logs.
Visual Concept
Transaction lifecycle
Create → Sign (wallet) → Broadcast → Pending → Mined / Reverted
Receipt snapshot
{
  transactionHash: '0xabc...',
  blockNumber: 12345,
  gasUsed: 21000,
  status: true
}
Key Takeaway

Transactions are paid operations. Validate inputs, estimate gas, and handle user and network errors to keep users safe.

screens.title: Call vs Send: Read-only calls and state-changing transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition. A call to a view or pure function is a read-only operation that does not create a transaction or alter blockchain state. It runs locally on an Ethereum node and is free. In contrast, using. send() on a contract method creates a signed transaction that is broadcast to the network, consumes gas, and can modify state. Concrete example: calling getStoredNumber() fetches the saved value without cost, while calling setNumber(42) with. send() writes the new value to contract storage and costs gas. A common misconception is that. send() is just a heavier call; it's fundamentally different because it requires a sender address and a signature. Another confusion arises when developers expect. send() to return the new state immediately — instead, it returns a transaction receipt only after the transaction is mined. Practical implication: only use. send() when you intend to change state. For testing, prefer local chains so you can iterate quickly; for production, design UX that explains gas cost and confirmation delay. Final takeaway: choose. call() for free reads and. send() for intentional, paid state changes, and design your UI to reflect that difference to avoid surprising users.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: .call() reads data for free; .send() creates a signed, gas-consuming transaction that changes state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Call vs Send
Definition

A call executes locally and returns values without creating a transaction. A send constructs a signed transaction that is broadcast and mined, modifying state and consuming gas.

Example: Read
const value = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getStoredNumber().call();
console.log(value); // free
Example: Write
await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(42).send({ from: currentAccount });
// costs gas, requires signature
Why it matters
  • Cost: calls are free; sends consume Ether as gas.
  • Identity: sends need the sender's account to sign the transaction.
  • Timing: sends require time to be mined; UI should show pending and confirmed states.
Key Takeaway

Use calls for reads and sends only when you need to change on-chain data. Always inform the user about gas and confirmation time.

screens.title: Constructing transaction parameters
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction parameters object tells the provider who signs, whether value is sent, and how much gas and fee to allow. The required field in practice is the from address: your connected account that will sign and pay for gas. If the target function is payable you must supply value, expressed in wei. Gas or gasLimit sets the maximum units of gas the transaction may consume; if set too low, the transaction will fail with an out-of-gas error. For networks using EIP-1559 you will use maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas instead of gasPrice. Concrete example: to send 0.1 ETH to a payable function use value: web3. utils. toWei('0.1','ether'). A common trap is supplying value in Ether instead of wei, resulting in huge or tiny transfers. Another common mistake is omitting from when the DApp hasn’t connected the wallet; this causes the provider to reject the request. Practically, assemble parameters after verifying the user's account and balance, estimate gas where possible, and include fee fields appropriate to the network. This creates predictable user prompts in MetaMask and reduces unexpected errors. Constructing transaction parameters means always set from; use wei for value; estimate gas and pick appropriate fee fields for the network.. In practical terms, from, value, gas, and fee fields explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always set from; use wei for value; estimate gas and pick appropriate fee fields for the network.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Transaction Parameters
Parameter breakdown
from
The signing address. Must be the connected wallet account used to pay gas.
value
Amount of Ether to send in wei. Use web3.utils.toWei('0.5', 'ether').
gas / gasLimit
Maximum gas units allowed. If too low the transaction fails; unused gas is refunded.
gasPrice / EIP-1559
Legacy gasPrice or EIP-1559 fields: maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas for modern networks.
Practical example
const tx = {
  from: currentAccount,
  value: web3.utils.toWei('0.1', 'ether'),
  gas: Math.floor(estimate * 1.2)
};
await contract.methods.deposit().send(tx);
Common mistakes
  • Specifying value in Ether instead of wei.
  • Failing to set from, causing provider rejection.
  • Not matching fee fields to the network’s fee model.
Tip

Detect the network type and choose gasPrice or EIP-1559 fields so MetaMask shows sensible defaults to the user.

screens.title: Estimating gas and adding a safety buffer
screens.narratorSegment: Estimating gas before sending a transaction is essential. Use the contract method's estimateGas function to get a realistic baseline. For example, call simpleStorageContract. methods. setNumber(newNumber). estimateGas({ from: currentAccount }) to obtain the expected gas usage. Because estimates can be optimistic or network conditions can vary, add a modest buffer — a common strategy is multiplying by 1.1 to 1.3 depending on complexity. Concrete example: if estimateGas returns 50,000, sending gas: Math. floor(estimateGas * 1.2) gives a safe upper limit. A common misconception is that the estimate always guarantees success; it does not protect against logical reverts inside the contract. Also note that adding too large a gas limit is wasteful only in the sense that it increases the gas cap, but unused gas is refunded — the user still pays only the gas used. Practically, perform a preflight estimate, show the estimated cost to the user (estimate * gasPrice or using EIP-1559 math), and include a small buffer. If estimateGas itself throws, handle it by informing the user and not prompting MetaMask, preventing a confusing failed transaction attempt. Estimating gas and adding a safety buffer means call estimategas, add a small buffer, and display estimated costs before prompting the wallet to minimize failures.. In practical terms, how to prevent out-of-gas failures and avoid wasting funds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas estimation
keyIdea.text: Call estimateGas, add a small buffer, and display estimated costs before prompting the wallet to minimize failures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Gas Estimation
Step-by-step
  1. Call estimateGas with the same from and parameters you will use.
  2. If estimate succeeds, compute a buffer: Math.floor(estimate * 1.2).
  3. Convert the estimated gas into an Ether cost for user display using gasPrice or estimated EIP-1559 fees.
  4. Include the buffered gas in the send parameters to reduce out-of-gas failures.
Example
const estimate = await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(newNumber).estimateGas({ from: currentAccount });
const gasLimit = Math.floor(estimate * 1.2);
await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(newNumber).send({ from: currentAccount, gas: gasLimit });
Pitfalls & UX
  • estimateGas can throw if the call would revert; do not prompt MetaMask then.
  • Large buffers avoid fails but set unrealistic caps; keep them conservative.
  • Show the estimated cost in ETH so users understand the charge.
Key Takeaway

Estimate gas, add a small buffer, and handle estimate failures before requesting a wallet signature.

screens.title: Signing and MetaMask flow
screens.narratorSegment: When you call. send() the provider opens a wallet confirmation UI where the user reviews the transaction parameters and either approves or rejects. The provider then signs the transaction with the user's private key; your app never sees the key. Practically, ensure currentAccount is set from eth_requestAccounts or eth_accounts before sending. A typical flow: 1) prepare transaction parameters with from and gas; 2) call contract. methods. myFunction(...). send(tx); 3) await the promise to resolve to a receipt when mined. Concrete example: calling setNumber triggers MetaMask to show gas and value; if the user clicks Reject MetaMask throws an error with code 4001. A misconception is thinking the wallet will always auto-fill gas optimally; wallets provide defaults but the DApp should estimate and present the user with a clear cost. For responsiveness, update the UI to a 'pending' state immediately after the wallet confirms, and poll or subscribe to receipt events to detect mining. Closing question: how will your UI distinguish 'pending' from 'failed' to give helpful next steps to the user? Signing and MetaMask flow means the wallet signs transactions; handle approval, rejection (error 4001), and present pending/confirmed states to users.. In practical terms, how the wallet requests a signature and what your dapp should expect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › MetaMask Flow
Typical sequence
  1. Prepare tx parameters and estimate gas.
  2. Call contract.methods.fn(...).send(tx) and wait for wallet popup.
  3. User approves: transaction broadcasts and returns a receipt when mined.
  4. User rejects: provider throws error with code 4001 — handle gracefully.
Code example
try {
  const receipt = await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(newNumber).send({ from: currentAccount, gas: gasLimit });
  console.log('Mined:', receipt.transactionHash);
} catch (error) {
  if (error.code === 4001) {
    console.log('User rejected the transaction');
  } else {
    console.error('Transaction error', error);
  }
}
UX recommendations
  • Show a clear pending state after user confirms.
  • Display transactionHash and let users copy or view details externally.
  • Handle user rejection without alarming language; offer retry guidance.
Misconception

Do not assume the wallet will auto-cancel or auto-retry for failures. Your app must detect and report outcomes clearly.

screens.title: Transaction receipt and confirmation status
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction receipt is the authoritative record returned after a transaction is mined into a block. The receipt includes the transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, status flag, and any emitted events. Use transactionHash to present a reference to the user; use status to determine whether the transaction succeeded or reverted. Concrete example: after calling send and awaiting resolution, your code receives a receipt where receipt. status is true on success. A common misunderstanding is relying only on the send promise resolving to mean business logic succeeded; if the transaction reverted its state changes were undone and gas was consumed, but the receipt will show a failed status or contract-specific logs that indicate a revert reason. For reliability, update UI only after the receipt indicates success, then call your read functions to fetch the new state. For additional assurances, you can wait for multiple confirmations (several blocks) to protect against chain reorganizations. Key practice: show the transaction hash to the user immediately and then update the displayed stored data only after reading the contract state from the chain. Transaction receipt and confirmation status means read transactionhash, status, blocknumber and gasused from the receipt and confirm state changes before updating the ui.. In practical terms, what the receipt contains and how to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Transaction Receipt
Receipt snapshot and meaning
{
  transactionHash: '0xabc...',
  blockNumber: 12345,
  gasUsed: 21000,
  status: true
}
Use transactionHash for references, status to check success, and gasUsed to audit costs. After receipt, refresh on-chain reads to reflect the new state in your UI.
Best practices
  • Show the hash immediately so users can track the transaction externally.
  • Wait for receipt.status === true before claiming success in your UI.
  • Consider waiting for additional confirmations if you need stronger finality guarantees.
Key Takeaway

Receipts are the definitive on-chain result. Use them to verify success, show hashes, and refresh your UI after confirmation.

screens.title: Common transaction errors and how to handle them
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions can fail for many reasons; categorizing them helps your DApp respond appropriately. First, user rejection: MetaMask throws an error with code 4001 when the user rejects signing. Handle this by showing a friendly message and leaving state unchanged. Second, insufficient funds: MetaMask or the node may emit an error saying the user lacks Ether for gas plus value. Mitigate by displaying account balances and performing preflight calculations before prompting the wallet. Third, out-of-gas: if the provided gas limit is too low the transaction executes until gas runs out and then fails, consuming gas. Prevent this by estimating gas and adding a buffer. Fourth, reverted transactions: contract require checks or revert calls will undo state changes but still consume gas; read receipt. status and any revert messages available from logs or from failing estimateGas to diagnose. Concrete example: catch errors around your send call and inspect error. code === 4001 for rejection, error. message. includes('insufficient funds') for balance issues, and receipt. status for success vs revert. Close with a reflective question: which of these failure modes will you surface to users immediately, and which will you pre-empt with checks?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Error Handling
Error types
User rejection (4001)
Handle calmly, show retry option and explain what the user rejected.
Insufficient funds
Preflight check account balance against estimated gas + value and warn before prompting.
Out of gas
Avoid by estimating gas; if it happens, report a clear failure message.
Reverted transactions
Detect via receipt.status and show possible reasons; log revert messages for debugging.
Handling pattern
  1. Preflight: validate input and check balance.
  2. Estimate gas and compute cost for display.
  3. Try send; catch errors and branch on error.code or message.
  4. On receipt, verify status and update UI or display revert info.
Example catch
try {
  const receipt = await method.send(tx);
} catch (error) {
  if (error.code === 4001) { /* user rejected */ }
  else if (error.message.includes('insufficient funds')) { /* warn user */ }
  else { /* log and show fallback */ }
}

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › setStoredNumber Example
Complete example
async function setStoredNumber(newNumber) {
  if (!simpleStorageContract || !currentAccount) {
    transactionStatus.textContent = 'Error: Contract not loaded or account not connected.';
    return;
  }

  if (newNumber === '' || isNaN(newNumber) || parseInt(newNumber) < 0) {
    alert('Please enter a valid positive number.');
    return;
  }

  transactionStatus.textContent = 'Estimating gas...';
  try {
    const estimate = await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(newNumber).estimateGas({ from: currentAccount });
    const gasLimit = Math.floor(estimate * 1.2);

    transactionStatus.textContent = 'Sending transaction... Please confirm in MetaMask.';
    const receipt = await simpleStorageContract.methods.setNumber(newNumber).send({ from: currentAccount, gas: gasLimit });

    transactionStatus.textContent = `Transaction successful! Hash: ${receipt.transactionHash.substring(0,10)}...`;
    await getContractData();
    newNumberInput.value = '';
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === 4001) {
      transactionStatus.textContent = 'Transaction rejected by user.';
    } else if (error.message && error.message.includes('insufficient funds')) {
      transactionStatus.textContent = 'Insufficient funds for transaction. Please top up your account.';
    } else {
      transactionStatus.textContent = `Transaction failed: ${error.message}`;
    }
    console.error('Error sending transaction:', error);
  }
}
Explanation and checks
  • Input validation prevents trivial reverts and bad UX.
  • Estimating gas before opening MetaMask avoids surprise failures.
  • Adding a buffer prevents marginal out-of-gas errors on complex state changes.
Key Takeaway

Follow validate → estimate → send → await receipt → refresh pattern and provide clear status messages for users.

screens.title: Safety, UX, and developer best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Safety and UX matter as much as correct code. Never handle private keys in your DApp — always rely on the user's wallet to sign transactions. Implement preflight checks: fetch the user's balance with web3. eth. getBalance(currentAccount), estimate gas for the intended call, and calculate the total cost (estimated gas * fee + value) to compare against the balance. Display friendly messages that explain why a transaction might fail and how the user can fix it, for example suggesting testnet faucets or instructions to top up Ether for test chains. For complex transactions, show a clear confirmation screen summarizing expected gas cost and the action's effects so the user isn't surprised. Instrument logs for failures and capture revert messages where available to speed debugging. Finally, provide retry paths and non-destructive fallbacks such as a dry-run or a read-only preview of the state changes. A common misconception is that more technical error text helps the end user — in reality, show human-readable guidance and log technical details to the console for developers. Safety, UX, and developer best practices means always preflight checks, never handle private keys, and present clear cost and retry guidance to users.. In practical terms, preflight checks, clear messages, and never handling private keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll move beyond reading contract data and learn how your DApp sends transactions that actually change state. Sending a transaction means creating a signed Ethereum transaction, paying gas, and waiting for the network to mine it. You'll learn what parameters are required — such as the sender address, value for payable functions, and gas limits — and how wallets like MetaMask participate by asking the user to sign. We'll walk through a practical example using a SimpleStorage contract's setNumber function, show how to estimate gas and add a safety buffer, and how to read the transaction receipt to confirm success. Along the way you'll learn common failure modes: user rejection, insufficient funds, out of gas, and reverted transactions, and how to present clear feedback to users. By the end you'll be able to implement a setStoredNumber workflow in your DApp that validates input, estimates gas, triggers MetaMask, monitors confirmation, and recovers gracefully from errors. Think about transactions as the paid, deliberate actions your users take on-chain — designing clear, safe flows reduces confusion and costly mistakes.

By the end of this chapter you will differentiate read-only contract calls from state-changing transactions, construct and send transactions from a connected wallet, specify the essential parameters like from, value and gas, and handle receipts and confirmations. You will know how to estimate gas, add a safety buffer, and read the transaction receipt to verify success. You will implement robust error handling for common cases such as user rejection, insufficient funds, out-of-gas, and reverted transactions. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone: sending a transaction to set a new value in SimpleStorage and updating the UI on success. These skills matter because they let your DApp move from passive data display to active, trust-conscious interactions that use real Ether and user signatures. As you learn, focus on clear user feedback and preflight checks to prevent costly mistakes and reduce confusion.

This second objectives screen focuses on the practical tasks you will complete. You will add an input and a trigger to your index. html and implement a setStoredNumber function in app. js that validates the input and interacts with the contract instance. You will estimate gas using the contract method's estimateGas call and then send the transaction with a small buffer added to the estimate. When the transaction completes, you will read the receipt to pull the transaction hash and block number and refresh displayed contract data. You will also handle user rejection (error code 4001) and provide clear status messages such as pending, success, rejected, or failed. These skills are essential because a DApp that performs state changes must be user-friendly, prevent wasted gas, and provide clear next steps after a transaction.

Start with a clear definition. A call to a view or pure function is a read-only operation that does not create a transaction or alter blockchain state. It runs locally on an Ethereum node and is free. In contrast, using. send() on a contract method creates a signed transaction that is broadcast to the network, consumes gas, and can modify state. Concrete example: calling getStoredNumber() fetches the saved value without cost, while calling setNumber(42) with. send() writes the new value to contract storage and costs gas. A common misconception is that. send() is just a heavier call; it's fundamentally different because it requires a sender address and a signature. Another confusion arises when developers expect. send() to return the new state immediately — instead, it returns a transaction receipt only after the transaction is mined. Practical implication: only use. send() when you intend to change state. For testing, prefer local chains so you can iterate quickly; for production, design UX that explains gas cost and confirmation delay. Final takeaway: choose. call() for free reads and. send() for intentional, paid state changes, and design your UI to reflect that difference to avoid surprising users.

A transaction parameters object tells the provider who signs, whether value is sent, and how much gas and fee to allow. The required field in practice is the from address: your connected account that will sign and pay for gas. If the target function is payable you must supply value, expressed in wei. Gas or gasLimit sets the maximum units of gas the transaction may consume; if set too low, the transaction will fail with an out-of-gas error. For networks using EIP-1559 you will use maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas instead of gasPrice. Concrete example: to send 0.1 ETH to a payable function use value: web3. utils. toWei('0.1','ether'). A common trap is supplying value in Ether instead of wei, resulting in huge or tiny transfers. Another common mistake is omitting from when the DApp hasn’t connected the wallet; this causes the provider to reject the request. Practically, assemble parameters after verifying the user's account and balance, estimate gas where possible, and include fee fields appropriate to the network. This creates predictable user prompts in MetaMask and reduces unexpected errors. Constructing transaction parameters means always set from; use wei for value; estimate gas and pick appropriate fee fields for the network.. In practical terms, from, value, gas, and fee fields explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Estimating gas before sending a transaction is essential. Use the contract method's estimateGas function to get a realistic baseline. For example, call simpleStorageContract. methods. setNumber(newNumber). estimateGas({ from: currentAccount }) to obtain the expected gas usage. Because estimates can be optimistic or network conditions can vary, add a modest buffer — a common strategy is multiplying by 1.1 to 1.3 depending on complexity. Concrete example: if estimateGas returns 50,000, sending gas: Math. floor(estimateGas * 1.2) gives a safe upper limit. A common misconception is that the estimate always guarantees success; it does not protect against logical reverts inside the contract. Also note that adding too large a gas limit is wasteful only in the sense that it increases the gas cap, but unused gas is refunded — the user still pays only the gas used. Practically, perform a preflight estimate, show the estimated cost to the user (estimate * gasPrice or using EIP-1559 math), and include a small buffer. If estimateGas itself throws, handle it by informing the user and not prompting MetaMask, preventing a confusing failed transaction attempt. Estimating gas and adding a safety buffer means call estimategas, add a small buffer, and display estimated costs before prompting the wallet to minimize failures.. In practical terms, how to prevent out-of-gas failures and avoid wasting funds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you call. send() the provider opens a wallet confirmation UI where the user reviews the transaction parameters and either approves or rejects. The provider then signs the transaction with the user's private key; your app never sees the key. Practically, ensure currentAccount is set from eth_requestAccounts or eth_accounts before sending. A typical flow: 1) prepare transaction parameters with from and gas; 2) call contract. methods. myFunction(...). send(tx); 3) await the promise to resolve to a receipt when mined. Concrete example: calling setNumber triggers MetaMask to show gas and value; if the user clicks Reject MetaMask throws an error with code 4001. A misconception is thinking the wallet will always auto-fill gas optimally; wallets provide defaults but the DApp should estimate and present the user with a clear cost. For responsiveness, update the UI to a 'pending' state immediately after the wallet confirms, and poll or subscribe to receipt events to detect mining. Closing question: how will your UI distinguish 'pending' from 'failed' to give helpful next steps to the user? Signing and MetaMask flow means the wallet signs transactions; handle approval, rejection (error 4001), and present pending/confirmed states to users.. In practical terms, how the wallet requests a signature and what your dapp should expect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A transaction receipt is the authoritative record returned after a transaction is mined into a block. The receipt includes the transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, status flag, and any emitted events. Use transactionHash to present a reference to the user; use status to determine whether the transaction succeeded or reverted. Concrete example: after calling send and awaiting resolution, your code receives a receipt where receipt. status is true on success. A common misunderstanding is relying only on the send promise resolving to mean business logic succeeded; if the transaction reverted its state changes were undone and gas was consumed, but the receipt will show a failed status or contract-specific logs that indicate a revert reason. For reliability, update UI only after the receipt indicates success, then call your read functions to fetch the new state. For additional assurances, you can wait for multiple confirmations (several blocks) to protect against chain reorganizations. Key practice: show the transaction hash to the user immediately and then update the displayed stored data only after reading the contract state from the chain. Transaction receipt and confirmation status means read transactionhash, status, blocknumber and gasused from the receipt and confirm state changes before updating the ui.. In practical terms, what the receipt contains and how to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transactions can fail for many reasons; categorizing them helps your DApp respond appropriately. First, user rejection: MetaMask throws an error with code 4001 when the user rejects signing. Handle this by showing a friendly message and leaving state unchanged. Second, insufficient funds: MetaMask or the node may emit an error saying the user lacks Ether for gas plus value. Mitigate by displaying account balances and performing preflight calculations before prompting the wallet. Third, out-of-gas: if the provided gas limit is too low the transaction executes until gas runs out and then fails, consuming gas. Prevent this by estimating gas and adding a buffer. Fourth, reverted transactions: contract require checks or revert calls will undo state changes but still consume gas; read receipt. status and any revert messages available from logs or from failing estimateGas to diagnose. Concrete example: catch errors around your send call and inspect error. code === 4001 for rejection, error. message. includes('insufficient funds') for balance issues, and receipt. status for success vs revert. Close with a reflective question: which of these failure modes will you surface to users immediately, and which will you pre-empt with checks?
